item.title: Digest — 22 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Gowers, Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao (guest post by Tristan Buckmaster) — Mathematics is a subject for the young

  • Expands his 19 October IAS talk. He returns to his "Deep Blue–Kasparov moment" comparison (made when he and Alpöge released their Euler result): OpenAI's Navier–Stokes proof reportedly took 10,000 agents running for 88 hours, a scale that is out of reach today but that falling costs could soon make widely available.
  • He argues that racing to be first on famous problems is over, but mathematics is not, because its value lies in human understanding: a machine-certified proof of RH would still leave open why it is true.
  • He sees mathematical physics as a natural target for AI: making heuristic physics rigorous, as Deng–Hani(–Ma) did for wave kinetic theory and for the Boltzmann equation (Hilbert's sixth problem), could become feasible for other effective theories.
  • Sharp criticism of AI companies: competing with their own customers, the 6 October OpenAI manuscript dump (some proofs unreadable or false, misleading compute claims, possible overlap with unreleased student work). He proposes zero-retention enterprise agreements covering every academic, opt-in-only training on user data, open-weight infrastructure, and a credit system that rewards exposition, disclosure and shared tools.
  • 👉 Directly relevant: AI and mathematical physics, plus concrete advice on data protection and credit that applies to PhD supervision.

Proofs and Prompts (Yiannis Sakellaridis) — Paralysis

  • He compares AI to a powerful new telescope for exploring mathematical truth, but warns against the alternative story in which machines do all the understanding, which in practice would mean subordination to the companies that own them.
  • He argues that AI firms need to capture scientific output as intellectual property to pay back trillions in investment, after training on publicly funded work released under non-commercial licences, and that their opacity makes "training off" settings impossible to verify.
  • His main charge is against the community: professional societies, institutions and advisory bodies have stayed silent on misconduct and IP theft, which he calls a "mathematical community in a state of paralysis". He also calls for public AI infrastructure for science.

Proofs and Prompts (Pavel Etingof & Slava Gerovitch, MIT) — Mathematics of the Future

  • Part of the 19–23 October series for PhD students and postdocs; a summary of a longer text. They argue that the four functions of mathematics (truth, culture, applications, intellectual growth) all survive AI, and that society should maintain mathematical expertise the way it maintains fire departments.
  • They expect the priority-based "ownership culture" to give way to evaluation based on intellectual agency: hiring through talks and direct conversation, and treating AI-assisted theorems the same as unassisted ones.
  • New roles they foresee: interpreting massive AI output, a "big cleanup" of the literature (fixing errors and gaps, plus Lean formalization alongside readable exposition), and richer publication formats. Teaching would add oral exams and value breadth over early specialization; a thesis need not contain a first proof.
  • Concrete proposal: small faculty-led labs where a group brainstorms, the AI responds to the notes, and students check and discuss the answers in a shared document. Advice to the young: accept uncertainty, learn broadly, collaborate.
  • 👉 Directly about PhD training and supervision; the lab model is worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts (Márton Balázs, Bristol) — The Power of Beauty and Elegance

  • He frames the "Ultimate Question" as whether brute knowledge and compute can beat human intuition for beauty and elegance in every area of mathematics.
  • He points out that most guidance on human-scale mathematics quietly assumes the answer is no. If it is yes, the profession becomes an exotic art with little funding, and the same would hold across science and engineering.
  • He remains optimistic, at least for many years, because LLMs still seem far from a useful sense of elegance for finding their way among possible theorems.

item.title: Digest — 21 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Gowers, Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — An experimental AI-math challenge: using tenth discriminant bounds to explore arguments ruling out Siegel zeroes

  • Tao launches an open, Polymath-style challenge: take each recent manuscript or write-up excluding Landau–Siegel zeroes (or proving a quasi-Riemann hypothesis) and use AI to extract an explicit upper bound on a hypothetical "tenth discriminant" in Gauss's class number one problem, without Heegner's method.
  • Background: Heilbronn–Linfoot's repulsion argument allowed at most one extra discriminant but was ineffective; Goldfeld (1976), then Oesterlé with the Gross–Zagier curve, made it effective. The new effective Siegel-zero arguments should each give such a bound, but making the constants explicit is tedious work well suited to AI.
  • Goals: compare the "strength" of competing write-ups, maybe a new Lean-formalizable (Mathlib-ready) solution of class number one, ideas for higher class numbers (solved up to 100 by Watkins), and possibly rescuing older failed attempts. Since the problem is solved, there's little risk of disrupting anyone's ongoing research.
  • Rules: any AI use allowed if disclosed, large outputs posted as GitHub links, outputs checked independently, credit given to earlier entries; quality over speed, and negative results (bad bounds) are welcome too. It follows his 19 October sketch of the Siegel-zero proof and his "Math 2.0" talk.
  • 👉 A concrete template for running AI-assisted collaborative research responsibly, worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts — Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?

  • An anonymous PhD student writes an open letter (part of a 19–23 October series for PhD applicants and students): after OpenAI's 6 October paper release, they have decided to leave academia after the doctorate.
  • The main argument: years of failing at hard technical problems are how a mathematician builds intuition and taste. A Math 2.0 where people curate and interpret AI output relies on experts trained the old way, and the letter says it never explains how it will train the next generation.
  • It also asks who such a profession will attract, and whether hiring and funding committees will reward slow independent work when peers turn out AI-assisted results.
  • Criticizes established mathematicians' enthusiasm, and Tao's Math 2.0 vision in particular, for ignoring what students want.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to PhD supervision: a clear statement of what some students fear.

Proofs and Prompts — A critique of the mathematical economy

  • Álvaro Gutiérrez (PhD student, Bristol) borrows Marx's labour theory of value to model mathematics as an economy: lemmas, proofs, examples, surveys and so on are "commodities".
  • He separates "true value" (the socially necessary labour time), use value (being reused in later work, which flows back to earlier papers), and realised value (referee reports, prizes, letters, jobs, grants).
  • LLMs cheapen all three: technical lemmas and counterexamples most of all, and attribution gets worse because models hide their sources. That fuels the fear that everyone must adopt AI to stay competitive, i.e. deskilling.
  • His twist: in mathematics there is no capitalist. Mathematicians themselves referee, hire and award prizes, so the community has more power than it thinks to decide what it values. He replies to David Bessis's "fall of the theorem economy".

Proofs and Prompts — Letter to a worried student

  • David A. Madore (Télécom Paris) publishes his email reply to a student wondering whether to leave mathematics, in English with the French original.
  • He shares the student's worries: AI companies treat open problems as trophies and a training ground, and say too little about their methods or their failed attempts for this to count as science.
  • He partly blames mathematicians themselves for prizing hard problems and races to results over understanding. He hopes research moves toward good questions, illuminating viewpoints and exposition.
  • His conclusion: understanding stays a human activity, and driving promising students away would be the worst harm AI could do to the field.
  • 👉 A voice from the French community, and a useful model for answering students who ask the same question.

item.title: Digest — 20 October 2026 (3 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new in the last 24 hours from Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Silicon Reckoner (Harris) or Tao's Mastodon.

Terence Tao — A sketch of the proof of non-existence of Siegel zeroes

  • Expository walk-through of the recent exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeroes, following Ben Green's streamlined version of a nine-page paper from OpenAI's math release (alongside two "quasi-Riemann hypothesis" papers giving zero-free strips with exponents 11/12 and 7/8). Banks (arXiv:2610.15483) and Kerr (arXiv:2610.21099) have produced their own digests.
  • Core estimate: primes with Legendre symbol (D/p) = −1 carry at most about half of the Mertens weight Σ log p / p; standard analytic arguments then recover the classical exp(−c√log x) error term without Siegel exceptions. Pescador and Barretto have sharper preprints.
  • Method ("adelic polynomial method"): take a lattice of integer polynomials, evaluate them with derivatives on a skewed grid of points m ± n√D, and study the integer M given by the squared covolume. Hadamard's inequality bounds |M| from above; Frobenius (the curve z₁^p = z₂ passes p-adically near every grid point when (D/p) = −1) forces large p-adic valuations; unique factorisation compares the two.
  • Non-degeneracy comes from a resultant argument exploiting the distinct second coordinates of the skew grid; Tao stresses the polynomial method is what breaks the parity barrier here, and asks readers for the history of the technique (Bombieri–Vaaler, Masser, Laurent).
  • Tao discloses that an AI chat helped him digest the preprints.

Proofs and Prompts — Recommendations on the use of AI for PhD students and supervisors

  • Guidelines from 37 symplectic geometers (incl. Auroux, Seidel, Smith, Keating, Cornea, Ginzburg), restricted to AI use for mathematical content, not editing or bibliography.
  • Students: engage with AI but verify every step yourself; keep a log of prompts and answers and disclose AI-derived content; AI is never a co-author; don't feed others' unpublished work to commercial models without consent. Expect more open-ended topics and higher standards of independence.
  • Supervisors: neither forbid nor impose AI; check whether a proposed problem could be dispatched quickly by a model; agree on documentation early; make sure core techniques and human contact are still learned; defenses should test real understanding of the new results.
  • Institutions: leave the choice of tools (commercial or local) to researchers, pay for them centrally, and set simple disclosure rules for theses.
  • 👉 Directly relevant: your field's community and PhD supervision; French signatories include Viterbo (Paris-Saclay), Oancea and Damian (Strasbourg), Gironella (Nantes), Mazzucchelli (Sorbonne).

Proofs and Prompts — Contribution, Credit, and Community

  • Tommaso Moraschini (philosophy, Barcelona) takes AI adoption as given and asks how credit should work afterwards.
  • Argues priority no longer signals insight and should stop counting as merit in itself; warns of a "Prompt or Perish" race, a flood of weak papers, and growing secrecy about partial results.
  • Considers AI disclosures unverifiable and liable to encourage concealment: comparable results should get equal credit whatever the tools, and abstaining from AI should not be rewarded.
  • Proposals: hiring that weighs exposition and vision (seminars, interviews, franker letters), and larger collaborative groups on exploratory programmes to defuse competition.
